records.source: דְּבַר־יְהוָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֔ה אֶל־יוֹאֵ֖ל בֶּן־פְּתוּאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: [The] word of Yahweh which came to Joel son of Pethuel.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}'s word came to Joel son of Pethuel.

L.1: The word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} which came to Joel son of Pethuel.

R.1: This is the message {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave to Joel son of Pethuel.

decisions.choice: the word of the LORD that came to Joel: the heading of the whole book
decisions.reason: The same heading opens Hosea, Micah and Zephaniah. It presents everything that follows, the lament over the locusts, the call to return, the promises and the judgment of the nations, as one message from the LORD given through one man.

decisions.choice: Joel son of Pethuel: the prophet, known only from this book; the book gives no date
alternatives: a date in the ninth century BC, in the reign of King Joash
a date after the exile, in the Persian period
decisions.reason: Nothing is known of Joel or his father Pethuel beyond this verse. The name Joel means "the LORD is God" and was common (1 Samuel 8:2; 1 Chronicles 5:4). Unlike Hosea, Amos or Micah, the heading names no king, and the book never mentions one. It speaks of the temple, its priests and the elders (1:9, 13-14), of Tyre, Sidon and Philistia selling people of Judah to the Greeks (4:4-6), and of Egypt and Edom (4:19). From these hints the book has been dated anywhere from the ninth century BC to after the return from exile, in the fifth or fourth century BC. Its message does not depend on the date.

decisions.choice: The word of the LORD which came to (L); The LORD's word came to (B); This is the message the LORD gave to (R)
decisions.reason: The heading follows the wording set for the Twelve, as in Hosea 1:1. Readable says "message" for "word" and turns the heading into a sentence.

records.heading: The locusts and the ruined land

records.source: שִׁמְעוּ־זֹאת֙ הַזְּקֵנִ֔ים וְהַֽאֲזִ֔ינוּ כֹּ֖ל יוֹשְׁבֵ֣י הָאָ֑רֶץ הֶהָ֤יְתָה זֹּאת֙ בִּֽימֵיכֶ֔ם וְאִ֖ם בִּימֵ֥י אֲבֹֽתֵיכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: Hear this, the elders, and give ear, all [the] inhabitants of the land! Has this been in your days, or in [the] days of your fathers?
pieces: Hear this, you elders! \q Listen, all who live in the land! \q Has anything like this happened in your days, \q or in the days of your ancestors?

L.2: Hear this, you elders, \q and give ear, all the inhabitants of the land! \q Has [anything like] this happened in your days, \q or in the days of your fathers?

R.2: Listen to this, you elders! \q Listen, everyone who lives in the land! \q Has anything like this ever happened in your lifetime, \q or in the lifetime of your ancestors?

decisions.choice: the elders: the old people of the community, who were also its leaders
decisions.reason: The word means old people and, from them, the leaders of a town or people. Here the prophet appeals to those whose memory goes back furthest: no one alive has seen anything like this. In 1:14 and 2:16 the same word is used of those gathered for the fast.

decisions.choice: the inhabitants of the land: the people of Judah
decisions.reason: The "land" here is the land of Judah, the LORD's land (1:6; 2:18), not the whole earth. The people addressed are those who live there and gather at the temple in Jerusalem (1:14).

decisions.choice: has this happened in your days or your fathers' days?: nothing like it has ever been seen
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer no. It recalls the locust plague of Egypt, which neither the fathers nor the fathers' fathers of the Egyptians had seen (Exodus 10:6, 14). Joel's disaster is described as being as great as that one.

decisions.choice: your ancestors (B, R); your fathers (L)
decisions.reason: "Fathers" here means the generations before, so Balanced and Readable say "ancestors". Readable says "in your lifetime" for "in your days".

records.source: עָלֶ֖יהָ לִבְנֵיכֶ֣ם סַפֵּ֑רוּ וּבְנֵיכֶם֙ לִבְנֵיהֶ֔ם וּבְנֵיהֶ֖ם לְד֥וֹר אַחֵֽר׃
records.gloss: About it to your children tell, and your children to their children, and their children to a generation another.
pieces: Tell your children about it, \q and let your children tell their children, \q and their children the generation after them.

L.3: Tell your children about it, \q and [let] your children [tell] their children, \q and their children [tell it] to another generation.

R.3: Tell your children about it. \q Let them tell their children, \q and let those children tell the people who come after them.

decisions.choice: tell: the one verb serves for the whole chain of generations
decisions.reason: The Hebrew uses the verb once and lets it carry through the next two lines: each generation is to pass the story on to the next.

decisions.choice: telling children and grandchildren: as the LORD's deeds in Egypt were to be told
decisions.reason: In Exodus 10:2, just before the locust plague, the LORD tells Moses to recount his deeds to his son and grandson. Psalm 78:4-6 speaks of telling the next generation the LORD's works. Here what must be remembered is a disaster, and what the LORD will do after it.

decisions.choice: children at every level
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word is the usual word for sons, used for children of both sexes; "children" says that at every level. Literal supplies "let" and "tell" in brackets, which the Hebrew leaves to be carried over from the first line.

records.source: יֶ֤תֶר הַגָּזָם֙ אָכַ֣ל הָֽאַרְבֶּ֔ה וְיֶ֥תֶר הָאַרְבֶּ֖ה אָכַ֣ל הַיָּ֑לֶק וְיֶ֣תֶר הַיֶּ֔לֶק אָכַ֖ל הֶחָסִֽיל׃
records.gloss: [What] remained of the cutting locust, has eaten the swarming locust; and [what] remained of the swarming locust, has eaten the hopping locust; and [what] remained of the hopping locust, has eaten the stripping locust.
pieces: What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten. \q What the swarming locust left, the hopping locust has eaten, \q and what the hopping locust left, the stripping locust has eaten.

L.4: What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten; \q and what the swarming locust left, the hopping locust has eaten; \q and what the hopping locust left, the stripping locust has eaten.

R.4: One swarm of locusts after another has come. \q What one swarm left, the next swarm ate, \q and what that swarm left, still another ate.

decisions.choice: four names for locusts: kinds of locust, stages of its growth, or simply four names for one plague
alternatives: four stages in the growth of one kind of locust
decisions.reason: The four words are the cutting locust (from a verb meaning to cut off), the swarming locust (the most common word for locust), the hopping or licking locust, and the stripping or finishing locust (from a verb meaning to consume). They may name different kinds of locust, or the stages through which a locust grows from a crawling young insect to a flying adult, or they may be four poetic names for the same insect. In 2:25 the four names come in a different order, which suggests that they are not a strict sequence. The point is plain either way: wave after wave came until nothing was left.

decisions.choice: a real locust plague, which stripped the land
decisions.reason: Swarms of desert locusts, in numbers beyond counting, can strip every green thing from a region in hours (Exodus 10:12-15). The law names locusts among the curses on a disobedient people (Deuteronomy 28:38, 42), and Solomon prays about them (1 Kings 8:37). The rest of the chapter describes the damage to vines, fig trees, grain and pasture. Some ancient readers took the four locusts as pictures of four enemy empires; the text itself speaks of locusts, which 1:6 and chapter 2 then describe as an invading army.

decisions.choice: the cutting locust, the swarming locust, the hopping locust, the stripping locust (L, B); one swarm of locusts after another (R)
decisions.reason: The names follow the wording set for the Twelve. Literal and Balanced give each name its own English word, so the reader can follow the chain and see it come back in 2:25. Readable does not name four kinds, which might settle a question the text leaves open (m1), and says what the chain means.

records.source: הָקִ֤יצוּ שִׁכּוֹרִים֙ וּבְכ֔וּ וְהֵילִ֖לוּ כָּל־שֹׁ֣תֵי יָ֑יִן עַל־עָסִ֕יס כִּ֥י נִכְרַ֖ת מִפִּיכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: Wake up, drunkards, and weep; and wail, all drinkers of wine, over [the] sweet wine, for it has been cut off from your mouth.
pieces: Wake up, you drunkards, and weep! \q Wail, all you who drink wine, \q because the sweet wine has been cut off from your lips.

L.5: Wake up, drunkards, and weep; \q and wail, all drinkers of wine, \q over the sweet wine, for it is cut off from your mouth.

R.5: Wake up, you drunkards, and cry! \q All you who drink wine, cry out in grief, \q because there is no more sweet wine for you to drink.

decisions.choice: sweet wine: the fresh juice of newly pressed grapes
decisions.reason: The word names new, sweet wine, the juice just trodden out of the grapes (Isaiah 49:26; Amos 9:13). With the vines stripped (verse 7) there will be no grape harvest. In 4:18 the same word returns in the promise that the mountains will drip with sweet wine.

decisions.choice: wake up, drunkards: the first to feel the loss are called to wake to the disaster
decisions.reason: The call to the drunkards has a bitter edge: they are told to wake from their stupor, and they are the first to notice that the wine is gone. The call to grieve then passes to the farmers (verse 11) and the priests (verse 13).

decisions.choice: Wail (L, B); cry out in grief (R); your lips (B)
decisions.reason: The call to wail follows the wording set in Isaiah: "Wail" at Literal and Balanced, "Cry out in grief" at Readable. Balanced says "lips" for "mouth"; Readable says plainly that the wine is gone.

records.source: כִּֽי־גוֹי֙ עָלָ֣ה עַל־אַרְצִ֔י עָצ֖וּם וְאֵ֣ין מִסְפָּ֑ר שִׁנָּיו֙ שִׁנֵּ֣י אַרְיֵ֔ה וּֽמְתַלְּע֥וֹת לָבִ֖יא לֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: For a nation has come up against my land, mighty and without number; its teeth [are the] teeth of a lion, and [the] fangs of a lioness [are] to it.
pieces: For a nation has invaded {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} land, \q powerful and too many to count. \q Its teeth are a lion's teeth; \q it has the fangs of a lioness.

L.6: For a nation has come up against {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} land, \q mighty and without number; \q its teeth [are] a lion's teeth, \q and it has the fangs of a lioness.

R.6: A nation of locusts has invaded {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} land. \q It is powerful, and there are too many to count. \q Its teeth are like a lion's teeth. \q It has fangs like a lioness.

decisions.choice: a nation: the locust swarm, pictured as an invading people
alternatives: a human army, foreshadowed by the locusts
decisions.reason: The word usually names a nation. Proverbs 30:25-27 calls ants and locusts "a people" in the same way. What this "nation" does in verse 7, stripping vines and fig trees, is what locusts do, so the swarm of verse 4 is meant, described as an army that invades the land. Chapter 2 develops the picture. Some readers take the nation as a human army that the locusts foreshadow.

decisions.choice: my land: the LORD speaks of the land as his own
alternatives: the prophet speaks for the people
decisions.reason: The speaker is not named. The land is called the LORD's land in 2:18 ("his land") and 4:2 ("my land"), and the vine and fig tree of verse 7 are "my" too, so the LORD most likely speaks here. The prophet may instead be speaking for the people, who would call it "my land" as well.

decisions.choice: teeth of a lion, fangs of a lioness: small insects that devour like the fiercest of animals
decisions.reason: Two words for the lion are used; the second may mean a lioness. A locust's jaws are tiny, but together the swarm devours as a lion tears its prey. Revelation 9:8 takes up the picture for its locusts.

decisions.choice: A nation of locusts
decisions.reason: Readable says that the nation is the locusts (m1), since a young reader would otherwise think of a human army.

records.source: שָׂ֤ם גַּפְנִי֙ לְשַׁמָּ֔ה וּתְאֵנָתִ֖י לִקְצָפָ֑ה חָשֹׂ֤ף חֲשָׂפָהּ֙ וְהִשְׁלִ֔יךְ הִלְבִּ֖ינוּ שָׂרִיגֶֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: It has made my vine into a waste, and my fig tree into splinters; stripping it has stripped it and thrown [it] down; white have become its branches.
pieces: It has laid waste {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} vines \q and turned {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} fig trees to broken stumps. \q It has stripped off their bark and thrown it down, \q and their branches are left white.

L.7: It has made {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} vine a waste \q and {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} fig tree a splintered stump; \q it has stripped off its bark and thrown it down; \q its branches have turned white.

R.7: It has ruined {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} grapevines \q and torn {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} fig trees to pieces. \q It has stripped off their bark and thrown it away. \q Now their branches are white and bare.

decisions.choice: vine and fig tree: the main fruit crops, and a picture of the people's life in the land
decisions.reason: The vine and the fig tree stand for a settled, peaceful life in the land (1 Kings 5:5; Micah 4:4) and are sometimes pictures of Israel itself (Hosea 9:10). When the leaves and fruit are gone, locusts gnaw the bark, and the branches are left bare and white.

decisions.choice: a splintered stump: a rare word, perhaps for something snapped off
decisions.reason: The word is found only here. It comes from a root that may mean to snap or break off, so it pictures fig trees snapped and splintered, or perhaps their bark peeled into shreds.

decisions.choice: my vine, my fig tree: the LORD's, as in verse 6
decisions.reason: The "my" continues verse 6: the land and its vines and trees belong to the LORD (see the note there).

decisions.choice: vines, fig trees (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew uses the singular for the whole crop. Balanced and Readable use the plural, which says the same thing in natural English; Literal keeps the singular.

records.source: אֱלִ֕י כִּבְתוּלָ֥ה חֲגֻֽרַת־שַׂ֖ק עַל־בַּ֥עַל נְעוּרֶֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: Lament like a virgin girded [with] sackcloth for [the] husband of her youth.
pieces: Mourn like a young woman dressed in sackcloth, \q grieving for the man she was pledged to marry.

L.8: Lament like a virgin wearing sackcloth \q for the husband of her youth.

R.8: Cry like a young woman wearing sackcloth \q because the man she was going to marry has died.

decisions.choice: lament: a command to one woman, the land or people pictured as a mourning bride
decisions.reason: The verb is a feminine singular command, and the word is found only here. The one addressed is not named: it is most likely the land, or Zion and its people, pictured as a woman in mourning.

decisions.choice: a virgin ... the husband of her youth: a young woman whose bridegroom has died before the marriage was complete
alternatives: a young wife mourning her husband
decisions.reason: The word for the woman names a young woman of marriageable age who has not yet married. In Israel a man pledged to marry a woman was already called her husband (Deuteronomy 22:23-24). So the picture is most likely of a young bride whose promised husband has died before the wedding. Others read it of a young wife whose husband has died.

decisions.choice: sackcloth: rough cloth worn in mourning
decisions.reason: Sackcloth was coarse cloth, often of goat's hair, worn next to the skin by those in mourning or in deep distress (Genesis 37:34; 2 Samuel 3:31).

decisions.choice: a young woman (B, R); the man she was pledged to marry (B); the man she was going to marry has died (R)
decisions.reason: Literal says "virgin" and "the husband of her youth". Balanced and Readable say what the picture means (m2). Readable says plainly that he has died, which the mourning implies.

records.source: הָכְרַ֥ת מִנְחָ֛ה וָנֶ֖סֶךְ מִבֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה אָֽבְלוּ֙ הַכֹּ֣הֲנִ֔ים מְשָׁרְתֵ֖י יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: Has been cut off grain offering and drink offering from [the] house of Yahweh; mourn the priests, ministers of Yahweh.
pieces: Grain offerings and drink offerings have ceased in the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q The priests grieve, \q those who serve {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.9: Grain offering and drink offering are cut off from the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; \q the priests mourn, \q the ministers of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.9: There is no more grain or wine to offer in the temple of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q The priests who serve {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} are mourning.

decisions.choice: grain offering and drink offering: the daily gifts offered with the morning and evening sacrifice
decisions.reason: Every morning and evening a lamb was offered with flour mixed with oil and with a drink offering of wine (Exodus 29:38-42; Numbers 28:3-8). With no grain, oil or wine, these daily offerings stop, and the regular worship of the temple is cut off.

decisions.choice: the house of the LORD: the temple in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The temple is called the LORD's house throughout the Old Testament. Joel speaks of it as standing and in use (1:13-14, 16; 2:17).

decisions.choice: ministers of the LORD: those who serve him
decisions.reason: The word means those who serve or attend on someone. It is used for the priests and Levites who served at the altar (Exodus 28:43; Jeremiah 33:21).

decisions.choice: no more grain or wine to offer in the temple
decisions.reason: Readable says what the two offerings were made of, and "temple" for "the house of the LORD".

records.source: שֻׁדַּ֣ד שָׂדֶ֔ה אָבְלָ֖ה אֲדָמָ֑ה כִּ֚י שֻׁדַּ֣ד דָּגָ֔ן הוֹבִ֥ישׁ תִּיר֖וֹשׁ אֻמְלַ֥ל יִצְהָֽר׃
records.gloss: Devastated [is the] field; mourns [the] ground; for devastated [is the] grain, dried up [the] new wine, fails [the] fresh oil.
pieces: The fields are laid waste; the ground is in mourning, \q for the grain is ruined, \q the new wine has dried up, and the olive oil has failed.

L.10: The field is devastated; the ground mourns, \q for the grain is devastated, \q the new wine has dried up, the fresh oil fails.

R.10: The fields are ruined, and the ground itself mourns. \q The grain is destroyed. \q There is no new wine and no olive oil.

decisions.choice: the ground mourns: grieves, and also dries up
decisions.reason: Two Hebrew verbs sound the same: one means to mourn, the other to dry up. Here the ground "mourns" just after the priests mourn (verse 9), and the drying of the crops follows. The word may be chosen to carry both: the parched ground looks like a mourner.

decisions.choice: grain, new wine and fresh oil: the three great products of the land
decisions.reason: These are the gifts the LORD promised to a faithful people (Deuteronomy 7:13; 11:14), and their loss is among the curses of Deuteronomy 28:38-40, 51. Hosea 2:10-11 names the same three. "New wine" is freshly pressed wine; "fresh oil" is newly pressed olive oil. The Hebrew of the first line also plays on sound: "devastated" and "field" begin alike.

decisions.choice: olive oil (B, R); fresh oil (L)
decisions.reason: As in Hosea 2:10, Literal says "fresh oil" and Balanced and Readable "olive oil". Readable puts the three losses simply, and keeps "mourns" (m1).

records.source: הֹבִ֣ישׁוּ אִכָּרִ֗ים הֵילִ֨ילוּ֙ כֹּֽרְמִ֔ים עַל־חִטָּ֖ה וְעַל־שְׂעֹרָ֑ה כִּ֥י אָבַ֖ד קְצִ֥יר שָׂדֶֽה׃
records.gloss: Be ashamed, farmers; wail, vinedressers, over wheat and over barley; for has perished [the] harvest of [the] field.
pieces: Be dismayed, you farmers! Wail, you who tend the vines, \q over the wheat and the barley, \q because the harvest of the field is lost.

L.11: Be ashamed, farmers; wail, vinedressers, \q over the wheat and over the barley, \q for the harvest of the field has perished.

R.11: Farmers, be sad and dismayed! You who grow grapes, cry out in grief! \q Cry for the wheat and the barley, \q because the harvest in the fields is ruined.

decisions.choice: be ashamed: be dismayed and disappointed, as when hope comes to nothing
decisions.reason: The verb is the usual one for shame. It is used of those whose hopes are disappointed (Jeremiah 14:3-4, of farmers in a drought). It sounds almost the same as the verb "dried up" in verses 10, 12 and 17, and the prophet plays on the two: the crops dry up and the farmers are put to shame.

decisions.choice: wheat and barley: the grain harvest
decisions.reason: Barley ripened first, in spring, and wheat some weeks later. Both are lost, so there is nothing to harvest at all.

decisions.choice: Be dismayed (B); be sad and dismayed (R); you who tend the vines (B); You who grow grapes (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "dismayed", the sense of "ashamed" here (m1), and describe the vinedressers' work.

records.source: הַגֶּ֣פֶן הוֹבִ֔ישָׁה וְהַתְּאֵנָ֖ה אֻמְלָ֑לָה רִמּ֞וֹן גַּם־תָּמָ֣ר וְתַפּ֗וּחַ כָּל־עֲצֵ֤י הַשָּׂדֶה֙ יָבֵ֔שׁוּ כִּֽי־הֹבִ֥ישׁ שָׂשׂ֖וֹן מִן־בְּנֵ֥י אָדָֽם׃ס
records.gloss: The vine has dried up, and the fig tree withers; pomegranate, also palm, and apple tree, all [the] trees of the field have dried up; for has dried up joy from [the] children of mankind.
pieces: The vine has withered, \q the fig tree droops; \q pomegranate, palm, and apple tree, all the trees of the field are dried up. \q Surely joy has withered away from the people.

L.12: The vine has dried up, \q and the fig tree withers; \q pomegranate, palm also, and apple tree, all the trees of the field have dried up; \q indeed, joy has dried up from the children of mankind.

R.12: The grapevines are dry, \q and the fig trees are dying. \q The pomegranate trees, palm trees, apple trees, and all the trees in the fields have dried up. \q And the people have lost all their joy.

decisions.choice: joy has dried up: the same verb as for the vine, with a play on "be ashamed"
decisions.reason: The verb used for the vine at the start of the verse is used again for joy at the end: the joy of the people withers with their trees. The same verb can be heard as "be put to shame" (see verse 11). Harvest was a time of great joy (Isaiah 9:2; 16:10), and now there is none.

decisions.choice: apple tree: perhaps another fruit tree, such as the apricot or quince
decisions.reason: The tree is named with the word for apple in later Hebrew, but it is not certain which fruit tree is meant in Bible times (Song of Songs 2:3; Proverbs 25:11).

decisions.choice: the children of mankind (L); the people (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew phrase, which means human beings. Balanced and Readable say "the people".

records.source: חִגְר֨וּ וְסִפְד֜וּ הַכֹּהֲנִ֗ים הֵילִ֨ילוּ֙ מְשָׁרְתֵ֣י מִזְבֵּ֔חַ בֹּ֚אוּ לִ֣ינוּ בַשַּׂקִּ֔ים מְשָׁרְתֵ֖י אֱלֹהָ֑י כִּ֥י נִמְנַ֛ע מִבֵּ֥ית אֱלֹהֵיכֶ֖ם מִנְחָ֥ה וָנָֽסֶךְ׃
records.gloss: Gird yourselves and lament, the priests; wail, ministers of [the] altar; come, spend the night in sackcloth, ministers of my God; for withheld from [the] house of your God [are] grain offering and drink offering.
pieces: Put on sackcloth and mourn, you priests! \q Wail, you who serve at the altar! \q Come, spend the night in sackcloth, you who serve my God! \q For grain offerings and drink offerings are kept back from the house of your God.

L.13: Put on [sackcloth] and lament, you priests; \q wail, ministers of the altar; \q come, spend the night in sackcloth, ministers of my God! \q For grain offering and drink offering are withheld from the house of your God.

R.13: Priests, put on sackcloth and mourn! \q You who serve at the altar, cry out in grief! \q You who serve my God, come and spend the night dressed in sackcloth. \q There is no grain or wine to offer in the temple of your God.

decisions.choice: gird yourselves: put on sackcloth
decisions.reason: The verb means to tie something around the waist. Its object is left out, but it is clear from verse 8 and from the same verb in Isaiah 32:11 and Jeremiah 4:8: the priests are to put on sackcloth.

decisions.choice: spend the night in sackcloth: mourning without a break
decisions.reason: To keep on the sackcloth even through the night was a sign of deep and urgent grief, as when David pleaded for his child (2 Samuel 12:16) and Ahab humbled himself (1 Kings 21:27).

decisions.choice: my God ... your God: the prophet speaks, and the God he serves is theirs
decisions.reason: "My God" is the prophet's own, and "your God" is the priests'. The same God is meant: the prophet calls the priests to lead the people in turning to him.

decisions.choice: Put on [sackcloth] (L); Put on sackcloth (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal supplies "sackcloth" in brackets; Balanced and Readable supply it plainly (m1).

records.heading: A call to fast and cry out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}

records.source: קַדְּשׁוּ־צוֹם֙ קִרְא֣וּ עֲצָרָ֔ה אִסְפ֣וּ זְקֵנִ֗ים כֹּ֚ל יֹשְׁבֵ֣י הָאָ֔רֶץ בֵּ֖ית יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵיכֶ֑ם וְזַעֲק֖וּ אֶל־יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: Consecrate a fast; call an assembly; gather [the] elders, all [the] inhabitants of the land, [to the] house of Yahweh your God, and cry out to Yahweh.
pieces: Proclaim a holy fast; call a solemn assembly. \q Gather the elders and all who live in the land \q at the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, \q and cry to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for help.

L.14: Set apart a fast; call a solemn assembly; \q gather the elders, all who live in the land, \q [to] the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, \q and to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} cry out.

R.14: Announce a holy fast, a time to go without food. Call everyone to a special meeting. \q Bring the elders and all the people of the land \q to the temple of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, \q and cry out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for help.

decisions.choice: consecrate a fast, call a solemn assembly: a holy day of prayer for the whole people
decisions.reason: To "consecrate" a fast is to set it apart as a sacred act. A solemn assembly was a gathering of all the people for worship, on which no work was done (Leviticus 23:36). In time of danger the king or leaders proclaimed such a fast, as Jehoshaphat did when enemies invaded (2 Chronicles 20:3-4).

decisions.choice: gather the elders, all the inhabitants: the elders and the whole people are called together
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets the two side by side without "and". They are most likely both gathered: the leaders and all the people (compare 2:16). The elders could instead be those who are told to gather everyone, "you elders, gather all the inhabitants".

decisions.choice: cry out: call for help in distress
decisions.reason: The verb is used for the cry of people in trouble to God (Exodus 2:23; Judges 3:9), the cry the prophet himself raises in verse 19.

decisions.choice: Proclaim a holy fast; call a solemn assembly (B); a time to go without food ... a special meeting (R)
decisions.reason: Readable explains what a fast and a solemn assembly were, and adds "for help" to "cry out" (m3). The same wording returns in 2:15.

records.source: אֲהָ֖הּ לַיּ֑וֹם כִּ֤י קָרוֹב֙ י֣וֹם יְהוָ֔ה וּכְשֹׁ֖ד מִשַׁדַּ֥ייָבֽוֹא׃
records.gloss: Alas for the day! For near [is the] day of Yahweh, and like devastation from [the] Almighty it comes.
pieces: Alas for that day! \q For the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is close at hand, \q and it will come like ruin from the Almighty.

L.15: Alas for the day! \q For near [is] the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q and like destruction from [the] Almighty it will come.

R.15: How terrible that day will be! \q The day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is near! \q It will come like ruin sent by God All-Powerful.

decisions.choice: the day of the LORD: the day when the LORD comes to act in judgment, and to rescue
decisions.reason: The prophets speak of a coming day that belongs to the LORD, when he steps in to put down all that is proud and wicked (Isaiah 2:12; 13:6, 9; Zephaniah 1:14-18). Amos warns those who long for it that it will be darkness for Israel, not light (Amos 5:18-20). Joel speaks of it five times (1:15; 2:1, 11; 3:4; 4:14). Here the locust plague is a sign that the day is near. In chapter 2 it comes as the LORD's army against Zion; after the people turn back to him, it becomes the day when the LORD judges the nations and saves those who call on his name (3:4-5; 4:14-17). The New Testament takes up Joel's words for the day of the Lord (Acts 2:20).

decisions.choice: the same words as Isaiah 13:6
decisions.reason: "Near is the day of the LORD; like destruction from the Almighty it will come" is found word for word in Isaiah 13:6, against Babylon (compare Ezekiel 30:2-3; Obadiah 15; Zephaniah 1:7). In Hebrew "destruction" (shod) and "the Almighty" (Shaddai) sound alike. Joel turns words spoken against a foreign power toward his own people.

decisions.choice: alas for the day: a cry of dismay
decisions.reason: The cry is the one Jeremiah and Ezekiel raise before God in dismay (Jeremiah 1:6; Ezekiel 4:14). Here it is raised over the day itself, whether the day of the present disaster or the coming day of the LORD named in the next line.

decisions.choice: the wording of Isaiah 13:6 at each level; Alas for the day (L, B); How terrible that day will be (R)
decisions.reason: Where Joel repeats Isaiah 13:6, each level uses the wording already published there: "near [is] the day of the LORD ... like destruction from [the] Almighty" (L), "close at hand ... like ruin from the Almighty" (B), "is near ... like ruin sent by God All-Powerful" (R). Readable says "God All-Powerful" for Shaddai, as the Isaiah table sets, and gives the meaning of the cry "alas".

records.source: הֲל֛וֹא נֶ֥גֶד עֵינֵ֖ינוּ אֹ֣כֶל נִכְרָ֑ת מִבֵּ֥ית אֱלֹהֵ֖ינוּ שִׂמְחָ֥ה וָגִֽיל׃
records.gloss: Is not before our eyes food cut off, from [the] house of our God joy and gladness?
pieces: Has not the food been cut off before our very eyes, \q and joy and gladness from the house of our God?

L.16: Is not food cut off before our eyes, \q from the house of our God joy and gladness?

R.16: We have watched our food disappear. \q There is no joy or celebration in the temple of our God.

decisions.choice: joy and gladness in the house of God: the harvest festivals
decisions.reason: At the festivals of harvest the people brought the first and best of their crops to the temple, ate before the LORD and rejoiced (Deuteronomy 12:7; 16:10-15). With no harvest there are no offerings and no feast.

decisions.choice: is not ... cut off?: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: The question states what everyone can see. The prophet now speaks with the people ("our eyes", "our God").

decisions.choice: statements in place of the question (R)
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into two plain statements, which say the same thing.

records.source: עָבְשׁ֣וּ פְרֻד֗וֹת תַּ֚חַת מֶגְרְפֹ֣תֵיהֶ֔ם נָשַׁ֨מּוּ֙ אֹֽצָר֔וֹת נֶהֶרְס֖וּ מַמְּגֻר֑וֹת כִּ֥י הֹבִ֖ישׁ דָּגָֽן׃
records.gloss: Have shriveled [the] seeds under their clods; desolate [are the] storehouses; torn down [are the] granaries; for has dried up [the] grain.
pieces: The seeds lie shriveled under the clods; \q the storehouses stand empty; \q the granaries are falling down, \q for the grain has withered.

L.17: The seeds have shriveled under their clods; \q the storehouses are desolate; \q the granaries are torn down, \q for the grain has dried up.

R.17: The seeds have dried up in the ground. \q The storehouses are empty. \q The barns are falling down, \q because there is no grain.

decisions.choice: the seeds have shriveled under their clods: three rare words, and an uncertain line
alternatives: a reading of the Greek: heifers stamping at their stalls
decisions.reason: The verb, the word for "seeds" and the word for "clods" are each found only here. The reading followed takes them as the sown seed drying up in the parched ground before it can sprout. The ancient translations understood the line very differently; the Greek translation, for example, speaks of heifers stamping at their stalls. The general sense, that the drought kills the crop before it grows, fits the verses around it.

decisions.choice: desolate storehouses, torn-down granaries: no grain to store, so the buildings fall into ruin
decisions.reason: With no harvest to put in them, the storehouses stand empty and the granaries are left to fall down. The last line repeats the play on the verb "dry up" and "be ashamed" (verses 10-12).

decisions.choice: barns (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "barns" for granaries.

records.source: מַה־נֶּאֶנְחָ֣ה בְהֵמָ֗ה נָבֹ֨כוּ֙ עֶדְרֵ֣י בָקָ֔ר כִּ֛י אֵ֥ין מִרְעֶ֖ה לָהֶ֑ם גַּם־עֶדְרֵ֥י הַצֹּ֖אן נֶאְשָֽׁמוּ׃
records.gloss: How groan [the] beasts! Wander in confusion [the] herds of cattle, for there is no pasture for them; even the flocks of sheep suffer punishment.
pieces: How the animals moan! The herds of cattle wander about in confusion, \q because they have no pasture; \q the flocks of sheep are suffering as well.

L.18: How the animals groan! The herds of cattle wander in confusion, \q for there is no pasture for them; \q even the flocks of sheep suffer.

R.18: Listen to the animals groan! The cattle wander around, confused, \q because they have no grass to eat. \q Even the sheep are suffering.

decisions.choice: suffer: bear the punishment of the land
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to bear guilt and its punishment. The animals have done no wrong, but they share in the punishment that falls on the land (Jeremiah 14:5-6; Hosea 4:3). A verb with almost the same letters means "be desolate", and some ancient translations read it that way.

decisions.choice: the animals: domestic herds and flocks with nothing to graze
decisions.reason: Cattle and sheep depended on open pasture. With the grass gone they wander in search of food. Their groaning joins the people's lament, as the wild animals' longing does in verse 20.

decisions.choice: Listen to (R); no grass to eat (R)
decisions.reason: Readable puts the exclamation "How ...!" as a call to listen, and says what pasture is.

records.source: אֵלֶ֥יךָ יְהוָ֖ה אֶקְרָ֑א כִּ֣י אֵ֗שׁ אָֽכְלָה֙ נְא֣וֹת מִדְבָּ֔ר וְלֶ֣הָבָ֔ה לִהֲטָ֖ה כָּל־עֲצֵ֥י הַשָּׂדֶֽה׃
records.gloss: To you, Yahweh, I call; for fire has consumed [the] pastures of [the] wilderness, and a flame has set ablaze all [the] trees of the field.
pieces: To {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, I cry out, \q for fire has devoured the pastures in the wilderness, \q and flames have burned up all the trees of the field.

L.19: To {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, I call, \q for fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness, \q and flame has burned up all the trees of the field.

R.19: {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, I am calling out to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} for help. \q Fire has burned up the grasslands, \q and flames have burned all the trees in the fields.

decisions.choice: I call to you, LORD: the prophet's own prayer
decisions.reason: The prophet now prays in his own voice, crying out to the LORD as he told the people to do (verse 14). His prayer closes the chapter.

decisions.choice: fire ... the pastures of the wilderness: drought and heat that scorch the land like fire
decisions.reason: The "wilderness" here is the open, uncultivated country used for grazing, not desert. The fire may be the burning heat of drought, which leaves the land as if burned, and grass fires in the dry fields may be meant as well. In 2:3 the locust army is also pictured as fire.

decisions.choice: LORD with no "O"
decisions.reason: The divine name spoken to God is written with no "O", as in the Psalms and the other prophets. Readable says "for help", the sense of the cry.

records.source: גַּם־בַּהֲמ֥וֹת שָׂדֶ֖ה תַּעֲר֣וֹג אֵלֶ֑יךָ כִּ֤י יָֽבְשׁוּ֙ אֲפִ֣יקֵי מָ֔יִם וְאֵ֕שׁ אָכְלָ֖ה נְא֥וֹת הַמִּדְבָּֽר׃פ
records.gloss: Even [the] animals of [the] field pant for you; for have dried up [the] channels of water, and fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness.
pieces: Even the wild animals long for {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, \q because the streams of water have dried up, \q and fire has devoured the pastures in the wilderness.

L.20: Even the animals of the field pant for {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, \q for the channels of water are dried up, \q and fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness.

R.20: Even the wild animals cry out to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, \q because the streams have dried up, \q and fire has burned up the grasslands.

decisions.choice: pant for you: the longing of a thirsty animal
decisions.reason: The same verb is used in Psalm 42:2: "As a deer pants for streams of water, so my soul pants for you, God." Here the wild animals, finding the streams dry, look to God for water.

decisions.choice: fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness: the last line repeats verse 19
decisions.reason: The repeated line closes the prayer and the chapter. The animals join the prophet's cry.

decisions.choice: streams of water: channels in the rock or the valley that normally carry water
decisions.reason: The word is used for watercourses and streambeds. The same word returns in 4:18, where the streambeds of Judah run with water again.

decisions.choice: wild animals (B, R); animals of the field (L)
decisions.reason: "Animals of the field" means wild animals, as Balanced and Readable say. Readable says "cry out" for "pant", the sense the parallel with verse 19 gives.
